name: Cultural bias
statement: Cultural bias is the error of reading a result obtained in one population as a fact about people, when the population sampled is an unusual one.
meaning: The everyday sense is judging another culture by the standards of one's own. The version that can be measured is narrower and belongs to research practice: a finding is collected in one population and written up as a finding about humans. Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan gave that version its name in 2010. Their abstract says behavioural scientists "routinely publish broad claims about human psychology and behavior in the world's top journals based on samples drawn entirely from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies". Researchers then assume, often implicitly, either that variation across populations is small or that these "standard subjects" are as representative as any other group. Their review covers visual perception, fairness, cooperation, spatial reasoning, categorisation and inferential induction, moral reasoning, reasoning styles, self-concepts and the heritability of IQ. The conclusion is that WEIRD subjects are "frequent outliers" and "among the least representative populations one could find for generalizing about humans". Two claims sit inside that and come apart under testing. One is about who gets sampled, which is a counting exercise and is settled; entry 82 carries the journal counts. The other is about whether it matters for any given result, which is an empirical question with a per-effect answer.

origin.who: Joseph Henrich, Steven J. Heine and Ara Norenzayan
origin.note: "The weirdest people in the world?", Behavioral and Brain Sciences 33(2-3), 61 to 83. The paper coined the WEIRD acronym and assembled the comparative evidence; it does not claim to have named the general problem, and credits Arnett's 2008 count of journal samples for the sampling figures it quotes.

evidence: The strongest cases in the review are ones where a low-level process was expected to be invariant and was not. Henrich and colleagues report Segall, Campbell and Herskovits's 1966 project on the Müller-Lyer illusion across 16 societies, 14 of them small-scale. The measure is the point of subjective equality, the percentage by which one segment must be lengthened before the two look equal. American undergraduates on average needed the segment about a fifth longer, the extreme of the distribution, and their value differs from every other society studied. The San foragers of the Kalahari showed a value that cannot be distinguished from zero, so the illusion is not an illusion for them. Henrich and colleagues note that many of the other populations cannot be distinguished from one another, and that the same pattern of population-level variation appeared for the Sander-Parallelogram and both Horizontal-Vertical illusions. Their second case is bargaining behaviour. Figure 3 of the paper reports dictator and ultimatum games run in 15 societies. The United States adult non-student sample has the highest mean dictator offer, nearly double that of the Hadza of Tanzania and the Tsimane of the Bolivian Amazon. In the ultimatum game the United States has the second highest mean offer, behind the Sursurunga of Papua New Guinea. On the punishment side, the income-maximising offer for the United States is tied with the Sursurunga and is five times higher than for 70% of the other societies. The authors' summary is that people from industrialised societies "consistently occupy the extreme end of the human distribution". A different kind of evidence concerns what authors then say about their samples. Rad, Martingano and Ginges coded every empirical article in Psychological Science for 2014, 223 original research articles yielding 428 studies and 450 samples. Fifty-one studies, 11.41%, gave no information from which the country or region could be coded. Of the remainder, 57.76% drew on samples from the United States and 94.15% sampled Western countries, counting English-speaking countries, Europe and Israel. Their harder finding is about bounding. Over 72% of abstracts carried no information about the population sampled, and 83% of studies reported no analysis of any effect of their sample's diversity. Over 85% did not discuss possible effects of culture and context on the findings, and 84% did not recommend studying the phenomenon in other cultures. Muthukrishna and colleagues put a number on the distances involved. They applied the fixation index from population genetics to the World Values Survey, treating questions as loci and answers as alleles, and built a scale of cultural distance from the United States. Japan and Norway come out similarly distant from the United States, at .115 and .124. Comparing survey regions inside the four largest populations, India has the largest mean regional diversity at .11, the European Union .09, China .05, and the United States .01.

replication.headline: Cross-population variation is large in the domains Henrich and colleagues reviewed and small in the 28 effects Many Labs 2 tested, where WEIRDness moderated three.
replication.detail: Many Labs 2 is the direct test, because it ran the same 28 preregistered protocols across many countries and then asked whether WEIRDness moderated any of them. The published abstract states that "exploratory comparisons revealed little heterogeneity between Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) cultures and less WEIRD cultures". The accepted manuscript gives the working. Samples were scored on a WEIRDness index built from country rankings and split at the mean. Slate 1 held 42 WEIRD samples against 22 less WEIRD ones, and Slate 2 held 44 against 17. For 13 of the 14 effects that were reliable and in the same direction as the original, the finding appeared in both WEIRD and less WEIRD samples "with similar effect magnitudes". The single exception was Huang, Tse and Cho's cardinal direction and socioeconomic status effect, where the less WEIRD samples showed no overall effect and wide variability. After correcting for multiple comparisons, three of the 28 effects showed evidence of moderation by WEIRDness: Huang and colleagues, Knobe's side-effect effect, entry 15, and Norenzayan and colleagues on formal versus intuitive reasoning. For Norenzayan, the cultural difference ran opposite to the original result. The project's own summary is that variability in observed effect sizes "was attributable more to the effect being studied than to the sample or setting in which it was studied". That is the finding that pulls against the review, and neither displaces the other. No single effect size stands for cultural bias, so the structured fields are left empty and the numbers stay per-effect.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490.

limits: Many Labs 2 sets out its own limits and they are the main ones here. The authors write that their approach "characterized cultural differences at the most general level possible", a dichotomy of WEIRDness, and "ignored the rich diversity within that categorization". The distribution is skewed. Their discussion says samples scoring above 0.70 were classed WEIRD, where the method section describes a split at the observed mean. On either reading the WEIRD samples are alike in WEIRDness and the less WEIRD samples vary widely among themselves. They add that a true examination "would need to more deliberately vary sampling across all dimensions" of the acronym. The analysis also does not address regional variation, such as the difference between American and British samples. Their sampling was wide in countries and narrow in kind, with 39 United States samples and 86 samples from 35 other countries and territories. None of the 28 effects was picked for being culture-sensitive, so the test asks whether WEIRDness moderates a slate of mostly Western social and cognitive findings, not whether the domains Henrich and colleagues reviewed vary. The two bodies of evidence also differ in what they sample: Segall's project and the small-scale-society economic games reached foragers, horticulturalists and pastoralists, and Many Labs 2 recruited through universities and online panels. Provenance is uneven. The Segall figures and the 15-society bargaining results are read off Henrich and colleagues' review. Segall's 1966 book and the underlying economics papers were not obtained, and the Cambridge copy of Henrich et al. (2005) returned an HTML challenge rather than a PDF. The Many Labs 2 published article is behind a 403 at the publisher. The text quoted here comes from the accepted manuscript in LSE Research Online, and the abstract from the publisher record. The two agree on every figure used above. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall and the open web in August 2026 found no second multi-site project that tested WEIRDness as a moderator across a comparable slate of effects.
misreadings: The first error is treating an unrepresentative sample as a refuted result. A sample that is unusual makes a claim about humans unsafe, and it does not make the claim false, which is why the question has to be settled effect by effect. Many Labs 2 settled it for 28 of them and mostly found no cultural moderation. The second error is reading less WEIRD as East Asian. Muthukrishna and colleagues note that the most commonly studied non-Western nations, Japan, Hong Kong and China, are nowhere near the extreme of their American scale. Japan sits about as far from the United States as Norway does. The third error is treating WEIRD as a synonym for Western. It names five dimensions, and the one large test of it collapsed them into a single country-level score, as its authors say in as many words. The fourth error is thinking a demographically varied American sample answers the objection. On the cultural fixation index the United States has the least regional diversity of the four largest populations measured, .01 against India's .11. The fifth error is confusing this entry with the counting exercise. How WEIRD the published literature is, and whether that has changed, is a question about journal samples and belongs to selection bias at entry 82.

sources.text: Henrich, J., Heine, S. J., & Norenzayan, A. (2010). The weirdest people in the world? Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 33(2-3), 61-83. Full text read from the authors' PDF at the University of British Columbia, which carries the target article together with the commentaries. The Müller-Lyer figures are Henrich and colleagues reporting Segall, Campbell and Herskovits (1966), and the bargaining figures are their description of their own Figure 3, drawn from Henrich et al. (2005, 2006, 2010).

Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490. The publisher's copy returns HTTP 403; the accepted manuscript was read in full at LSE Research Online and the published abstract at the OpenAlex record for the DOI. The manuscript's own abstract says nine effects had a tau near .10 where its discussion and the published abstract say eight; nothing quoted here depends on that count.

Full text read at PubMed Central, PMC7357184.

Jones, B. C., DeBruine, L. M., Flake, J. K., et al. (2021). To which world regions does the valence-dominance model of social perception apply? Nature Human Behaviour, 5(1), 159-169. Accepted manuscript read at Strathprints. Its abstract records 11 world regions, 41 countries and 11,570 participants, and reports that the model generalised across regions under the original analysis strategy and generalised much less under a method allowing correlated dimensions. Cited as a second cross-regional test rather than for any figure above.
